title: Aramaic beside Hebrew: sounds and first words

objectives.can: Recognise the regular consonant correspondences between Aramaic and Hebrew words, and keep the two languages' words apart.

explanation.summary: Aramaic and Hebrew are sister languages written in one script, and many of their words are the same word in two forms. A handful of regular sound changes lets you see the family likeness, but each language's word stands on its own: learn the Aramaic word as Aramaic.

sections.heading: Sister languages, one script
body: Hebrew and Aramaic belong to the same family of languages, the Semitic family, and they share many roots, endings and ways of building words. A reader who knows Hebrew will often see an Aramaic word and think of a Hebrew one. This lesson shows when that is a good guide and when it is not.

A word in Aramaic and a word in Hebrew that come from the same older word are called cognates. Cognates are not the same word. They often have different consonants, different vowels, and sometimes a different range of meanings. In this library the Aramaic words and the Hebrew words are separate headwords, and what you learn of one does not count as knowing the other.

sections.heading: Four consonants that change
body: Where Hebrew and Aramaic have the same older consonant, they sometimes write it with different letters. Four such correspondences are regular enough to learn. The first six rows of the table show them in real words.

Aramaic has dalet where Hebrew has zayin: the word for 'gold' in Daniel 2:32 and the word for 'this' in Daniel 2:18. Aramaic has tav where Hebrew has shin: the word for 'three' in Daniel 6:11 and the verb 'sat' in Daniel 7:9. Aramaic has ṭet where Hebrew has tsade, as in the verb 'took counsel together' in Daniel 6:8. And Aramaic has ayin where Hebrew has tsade, as in the word for 'the earth' in Daniel 2:35.

These are tendencies of the two languages, not rules that turn one into the other. The Aramaic word for 'heavens' in Daniel 2:18 keeps its shin, for example, and many Aramaic words with dalet, tav, ṭet or ayin have the same letter in Hebrew. A Hebrew tsade has more than one Aramaic outcome (ṭet, ayin, and sometimes tsade itself), so you cannot predict the Aramaic from the Hebrew letter alone. Treat the correspondences as a way to recognise a family likeness after you meet a word, not as a tool for guessing.

sections.heading: Vowels, endings and small differences
body: The vowels differ more than the consonants. A syllable that ends in a vowel (an open syllable) before the stress often keeps a full vowel in Hebrew and a shewa in Aramaic. The first vowel of the word for 'gold' shows this: Aramaic has a shewa, Hebrew a qamets. The first vowel of the word for 'heavens' shows it too.

Several smaller differences recur. The Aramaic word for 'one' has no alef at its start. Aramaic often has ā where Hebrew has ō. And the plural of masculine nouns ends in -ין in Aramaic and -ים in Hebrew: compare the Aramaic plural of the word for 'king' in Daniel 2:21 with the Hebrew plural. The Aramaic plural ending is taught in lesson A1.1.1.

Some words are alike in the two languages: the word for 'king' has the same consonants and vowels in both, in the absolute state. Do not take that as a rule: many pairs differ in every letter, and some Aramaic words have no usual Hebrew counterpart at all.

sections.heading: Keeping the two languages apart
body: A cognate can mean something a little different. The Aramaic verb in Daniel 3:1 means 'make', as in 'made an image'. The Hebrew verb with the same letters means 'work' or 'serve', and Hebrew uses another verb for 'make'. The Aramaic verb for 'see' in Daniel 2:31 has a Hebrew cognate that is used mostly of seeing visions; the ordinary Hebrew word for 'see' is a different verb. In both cases the Aramaic meaning must be learned from Aramaic.

So the approach of this course is: learn each Aramaic word from its Aramaic uses, and use Hebrew as a comparison only after you have the Aramaic word. When a lesson compares, it names the Hebrew word and says that it is Hebrew.

misunderstandings: A cognate is not the same word. The Aramaic word has its own spelling, its own vowels and sometimes its own meaning; learning the Hebrew word does not mean you know the Aramaic one.
The consonant correspondences are tendencies, not rules. Aramaic keeps shin in some words and has tav in others, and a Hebrew tsade has more than one Aramaic counterpart.
Aramaic is not Hebrew with different endings. It has its own verb system, its own way of marking a determined noun and its own particles, which later lessons teach.
Do not guess an Aramaic word's meaning from a Hebrew look-alike. Check it against the Aramaic text and the library's gloss.

deeper.heading: Why the letters differ
body: The twenty-two-letter alphabet was made for a language with fewer consonants than the older Semitic ancestor of Hebrew and Aramaic had. In the two daughter languages, several older sounds merged, and they merged in different ways. That is why one Hebrew letter can answer to several Aramaic ones. The details belong to historical grammar, and they are mentioned here only so that the correspondences in the table are not mistaken for arbitrary changes.

check.explain: Aramaic often reduces the vowel of an open syllable before the stress to a shewa where Hebrew keeps a full vowel. It is not a mistake and not a sign of a state. The consonants are not involved.

reading.why: Daniel's description of the great image uses gold, one, and the earth, three words of this lesson's table, in five verses of plain narrative. Read for the Aramaic words and notice, once, the Hebrew cognates; do not translate from the Hebrew.
